tagline.text: Three lagoons carved into a coral reef off Balaoan

location.label: Location
location.text: Offshore of Barangay Paraoir, Balaoan, La Union

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~900 (per person, on-site costs excluding transport)

children.text: Immuki Island is a coral reef flat off Barangay Paraoir in Balaoan, La Union, where you walk across at low tide or ride a raft at high tide to reach three clear lagoons. It is a short drive north of San Juan, making it an easy day trip during a surf holiday.

Immuki Island lies just off Barangay Paraoir in the municipality of Balaoan in northern La Union. Despite the name, it is not a sandy island but a reef flat of old coral that has hardened and risen above the sea. Hollows in the reef trap seawater and form three lagoons, and these lagoons are the main attraction.

Travel media have been presenting the place as a new La Union attraction since around 2018. If the surf beaches of San Juan and San Fernando are known for their waves and café scene, Immuki is about swimming, snorkeling and cliff jumping in calm, clear, nearly wave-free water. It suits anyone who wants to fill one day in La Union with something different.

The site is managed by the village community. One travel guide says it belongs to a marine protected area network set up jointly by Balaoan, Bacnotan and San Juan, and that visitors' entrance fees go toward clean-ups and mangrove care. Paraoir is also known for sea urchin farming, and tasting urchin locally is said to be possible. Operating rules and fees can change from year to year, so check the latest announcements before you go.

This guide does not claim to know where the name comes from. One guide says it derives from an Ilocano word meaning a gap or opening and adds that the area was once called Kaparingitan, but that rests on a single source, so treat it as a reference only. What is certain is that this is a community-managed site where you must register at the village, and the more you follow local guidance and the tides, the safer and more enjoyable your visit will be. A half day is enough, so it fits easily into a San Juan or San Fernando itinerary.
The first, second and third lagoons follow one another across the reef. The first is the widest and deepest, reported at around
3 m
at high tide, the second is a little shallower, and the third faces the open sea and feels darker and more enclosed. The water is clear enough that you can see the coral on the bottom.

blocks.title: On foot at low tide, by raft at high tide

children.text: When the tide is out, you can walk from the shore across the reef, and in the afternoon when the water rises you move by bamboo raft (balsa) poled by local residents. Some rafts have a roof and a table in the middle, so you can rest in the shade while touring the lagoons. Rafts often carry five or six people, so splitting the fee within your group keeps the cost down.

Inside the lagoons you can see small tropical fish and others moving among the coral. It is safer to bring your own gear, though many visitors report that life vests, goggles and similar items can be rented on site.

Many people jump into the water from the rocks on the edge of the second lagoon. Depth changes greatly between high and low tide, so always ask a local guide which spots and which times are safe before you jump.

Several mangrove species grow along the edge of the reef, and the fishers of Paraoir have raised sea urchins for many years. Visits to the urchin farm and tastings are described as an experience you request separately through the village fisherfolk cooperative.

The site faces the western sea, so the evening sky reflects off the color of the lagoons. Many people say the water photographs best in the early morning when few people are around, so photographers should go early. After sunset, however, the reef becomes dark and slippery, so decide your last move-out time beforehand.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Touring the lagoons on the low tide

children.text: Leave your San Juan or San Fernando lodging and head to Paraoir in Balaoan. Look for the Immuki entrance sign on the national highway and turn in. The ride takes about
30 minutes
Register at the information post near the Paraoir barangay hall and pay the entrance fee. This is also when you decide whether to hire a guide and whether you need a raft.
Check the tide, and if the water is low, walk across the reef to the first lagoon. Aqua shoes are essential.
Swim and snorkel in the first lagoon. Use the cliff spot at the second lagoon only as your guide directs.
Head back to the mainland before the water rises. Nothing is sold on the islet, so eat lunch in town or at a coastal restaurant.
Walking across in the early morning only works if the tide cooperates. Actual low-tide times change every day, so check a tide table first.
Arrive at Paraoir, register and rent a raft. In the afternoon the water is often high, so a raft is the practical way to get around.
Tour the lagoons by raft, swim and take photos. Rafts are often rented in blocks of about
1 hour 30 minutes
As the sun gets lower, watch the sunset from the reef. Return and pack up before it gets dark.
Head to a nearby coastal restaurant or back to San Juan for dinner.
The usual way is to take a northbound bus toward Vigan or Laoag from Pasay or Cubao in Manila and get off at Balaoan or Bacnotan. Travel guides say it takes roughly 5 to 7 hours via TPLEX.
Bus companies such as Partas, Viron and Dominion serve this route. Whether a trip stops there differs by departure, so tell the driver your drop-off point when you board.
From the Balaoan town center, continue to Paraoir by tricycle or jeepney. Ask to be dropped in front of the Paraoir barangay hall.
Bus times and fares change often, so confirm them at the terminal.
Take NLEX, SCTEX and TPLEX north, then pass San Fernando La Union and San Juan to reach Balaoan. Traffic makes a big difference, but it is safest to plan on about half a day.
A sign reading "Immuki Island" stands beside the national highway, so the way is easy to find. Parking has come up in local news, so follow the instructions on site.

items.title: From San Juan or San Fernando

children.text: From San Juan to Immuki, it is described as about
30 minutes
by tricycle or car.
For a cheaper route, take a northbound jeepney to Bacnotan and then a tricycle to Paraoir. One guide gives the fares for this route as roughly

Reports say that chartering a tricycle from San Juan for the day, with the driver waiting, runs around
. The price can change with bargaining.
For calm, clear water, the dry season from December to April is best. Winds are relatively light then and visibility is good, which suits snorkeling.

In the rainy season from June to October, typhoons and high waves can restrict entry or cloud the water. Always check the weather and local announcements before you leave. Within a day, the tide matters most. You walk at low tide and ride a raft at high tide, so the scenery and depth can differ greatly even on the same day.

Many guides say no food is sold on Immuki and that bringing food in is restricted. Some visitors report that small stores near the entrance sell drinks and snacks, so prepare the water and cash you need beforehand. One guide says there is no ATM in the village, so carry small bills. It is more practical to eat in Balaoan or Bacnotan town or at a coastal restaurant in San Juan, where you can try Ilocano treats such as bibingka and local seafood.

Most lodging is in the Elyu area of San Juan or in San Fernando rather than right at Immuki. The choices range from surf lodges and guesthouses to hotels, and Immuki is about 30 minutes away. A beachfront stay on the Bacnotan side shortens the trip further. Book ahead for peak-season weekends.

It is easiest to plan meals along your route. Around the town markets of Balaoan and Bacnotan there are local eateries and snack shops, and on the San Juan side cafés and seafood restaurants popular with surfers line the beach road. One guide says the Paraoir fisherfolk cooperative can arrange urchin tastings, but they are not sold at all times, so ask whether it is possible when you register. Urchin is eaten raw, so skip it if you are not feeling well.
Aqua shoes or thick-soled footwear are essential. Reviews consistently say the dead coral is sharp and going barefoot is dangerous, and staff may check at the entrance.
Check high and low tide times on a tide app or tide table before you go. The window when you can walk across differs from the window when you need a raft.
If it is your first visit, hiring a guide is safer. Signage is limited and the rocks are slippery.
Bringing your own snorkeling gear gives peace of mind. Renting a life vest on site is enough.
Carry plenty of small bills and change. The entrance fee, raft and shower are all paid in cash.
Guides mention local rules to reduce single-use plastic, so bring your own water bottle and a bag for trash.
To protect the coral, do not stand on living coral, and do not take shells, coral or marine life away.
If you care about photos, early morning on a weekday, when few people are around, is best.
The reef is sharp and slippery, and at high tide the water suddenly gets deeper. Always wear shoes, and put life vests on weak swimmers and small children.
Entry can be closed when a typhoon or high waves are forecast. Plans can change without notice, so leave some slack.
Cliff jumping without checking the depth and the coral below can lead to serious injury. Follow your guide's instructions.
Fees, hours and access rules differ by source and change. Rely on the signs on site and what barangay staff tell you.
There is almost no shade, so sunburn and heat stroke are risks at midday. You need a hat, long sleeves and water.
Do not leave valuables on the raft or reef while you swim, and bring only the minimum. A waterproof pouch is recommended.
Some guides say the site is not recommended for children under five or for people with limited mobility. For a family trip, stay mostly in the shallow areas at low tide.
La Union's best-known beach, famous for surfing and cafés, about
30 minutes
away by road and a good place to base yourself.
You can pair the capital's historic district and coastal scenery into a one-day outing.
A Spanish colonial-era watchtower on the Balaoan coast in Barangay Almeida, said to be good to visit together with the sunset view.
